terms.english: Who? Which one? (gen. τίνος, dat. τίνι, acc. τίνα)

examples.greek: τίς ἄρα οὗτός ἐστιν ὅτι καὶ ὁ ἄνεμος καὶ ἡ θάλασσα ὑπακούει αὐτῷ;
examples.english: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

examples.greek: ὑμεῖς δὲ τίνα με λέγετε εἶναι;
examples.english: But you — who do you say that I am?
What do you want me to do for you?

examples.greek: τί δειλοί ἐστε; οὔπω ἔχετε πίστιν;
examples.english: Why are you afraid? Have you still no faith?
Where did this man get these things?

examples.greek: πόθεν τούτους δυνήσεταί τις ὧδε χορτάσαι ἄρτων ἐπ' ἐρημίας;
examples.english: From where will anyone be able to feed these people with bread here in the wilderness?

examples.greek: ποῦ ἐστιν τὸ κατάλυμά μου ὅπου τὸ πάσχα μετὰ τῶν μαθητῶν μου φάγω;
examples.english: Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?

examples.greek: ποῦ θέλεις ἀπελθόντες ἑτοιμάσωμεν ἵνα φάγῃς τὸ πάσχα;
examples.english: Where do you want us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?
Tell us, when will these things be?

examples.greek: οὐκ οἴδατε γὰρ πότε ὁ καιρός ἐστιν.
examples.english: For you do not know when the time is.

examples.greek: καὶ πῶς πάσας τὰς παραβολὰς γνώσεσθε;
examples.english: Then how will you understand all the parables?

examples.greek: πῶς λέγουσιν οἱ γραμματεῖς ὅτι ὁ χριστὸς υἱὸς Δαυίδ ἐστιν;
examples.english: How do the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David?

examples.greek: διὰ τί οἱ μαθηταὶ Ἰωάννου καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ τῶν Φαρισαίων νηστεύουσιν, οἱ δὲ σοὶ μαθηταὶ οὐ νηστεύουσιν;
examples.english: Why do John's disciples and the Pharisees' disciples fast, but your disciples do not fast?
Why did you not believe him?

principles: τίς (who) is used for persons; τί (what) is used for things and can mean 'why'
πόθεν (from where) indicates source; ποῦ (where) indicates location; ποῖ (to where) indicates direction
πότε (when) asks about time; πῶς (how) asks about manner; διὰ τί (why) asks about reason
sheets.drill_instruction: Circling Drill: Take any verse from Mark and ask all the interrogative questions about it — τίς ἐποίησεν; τί ἐποίησεν; ποῦ; πότε; πῶς; διὰ τί; The information is not the point; the repetition builds fluency.

examples.english: By what authority are you doing these things?
Which commandment is first of all?
What sort of stones and buildings are these?
How many loaves do you have?

examples.greek: πόσος χρόνος ἐστὶν ὡς τοῦτο γέγονεν αὐτῷ;
examples.english: How long has it been since this happened to him?
How often shall my brother sin against me?
What large letters I have written!

examples.greek: τί ἐστιν εὐκοπώτερον; ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι, ἢ ἔγειρε;
examples.english: Which is easier: to say 'your sins are forgiven' or to say 'Rise'?

principles: ποῖος agrees like adjectives and asks about quality/type
πόσος asks about quantity or duration
ποσάκις (adverb) asks about frequency or repetition
πηλίκος asks about size or importance
ποδαπός asks about origin or classification
sheets.drill_instruction: Circling Drill: Extend drill from Sheet 2 to include these adjective-based questions: ποῖος; πόσος; πηλίκος; ποδαπός. Use with different subjects and direct objects to build broader interrogative fluency.

sheets.description: The first layer of fluency is social, not grammatical. Say these before you understand them — they are the phrases that let you stay in a Greek-only room without switching back.

terms.english: Thank you (lit. I give thanks to you)
I am glad you are well
By no means, not at all
Say it to me in Greek

principles.title: χαῖρε as imperative
principles.explanation: χαῖρε is an imperative — literally 'rejoice!' Greek greeting is a command to be glad. The reply is simply χαῖρε καὶ σύ.

sheets.drill_instruction: Practice greetings in context: meeting someone, parting, asking how they are, responding to questions about origins and names. All interaction must stay in Greek — use language phrases to ask for clarification rather than switching to English.

sheets.description: Essential classroom language for asking permission, requesting repetition, checking understanding, and managing comprehension in Greek-only environments.

examples.english: Is it permitted or not permitted?

terms.english: I want to ask you something.

examples.english: they said the same thing to him
he cried out with a loud voice
Do you understand all these things?

terms.english: What part of speech is it?

examples.english: he said, I do not know
they had forgotten to bring bread
Let us go to the next towns

terms.english: It is finished / that's the end.

examples.english: they have come to an end

principles: The subjunctive mood (ἄγωμεν, ἀρξώμεθα) expresses cohortative wishes: 'let us...'
τί vs ποῖος: τί (what?) for identity or substance; ποῖος (what kind?) for quality or category
In Greek-only instruction, these phrases keep learners engaged without resorting to English metalanguage
sheets.drill_instruction: Circle-and-Ask Drill: Take any verse and circle out with questions: τίς; τί ἐποίησεν; ποῦ; πότε; διὰ τί; The information is secondary; the repetition builds neural pathways. Start with simple narratives (Mark's healing stories) where concrete objects invite questions.

sheets.description: Imperative commands for classroom management paired with vocabulary for people, writing materials, furniture, and spatial relationships in the learning environment.

examples.english: Listen to the voice of the Lord
there was a certain female disciple
in the book of the law
at the door of the school

principles: Imperative mood distinguishes by number and voice: ἄκουε (sg.) vs ἀκούετε (pl.); ἔγειρε (active) vs ἀνάστηθι (middle/deponent)
Total Physical Response (TPR) drills use commands without translation: the body demonstrates understanding before the mind explains it
Spatial prepositions with the genitive (ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης), dative (παρὰ τῇ θύρᾳ), and accusative (ὑπὸ τὴν κλίνην) encode different meanings
sheets.drill_instruction: Total-Physical-Response (TPR) Drill: The teacher commands; the class obeys in silence. Example sequence: ἔγειρε· ἐλθὲ πρὸς τὴν θύραν· ἄνοιξον τὴν θύραν· κάθισον. No translation, no explanation. Comprehension shows up in the body first, then language follows.

sheets.description: Essential vocabulary for expressing hunger, thirst, food requests, eating preferences, and dining actions in everyday conversation.

examples.english: I am thirsty and have nothing to drink

terms.english: I am not hungry any more.
I do not want to eat.
It is good; it is delicious.
I am going off to eat.

principles: δός (aorist imperative) asks for the thing once, one specific request — pass me the bread. δίδου (present imperative) asks for it habitually — keep giving me bread. Mark's aorist imperatives are almost always the single, decisive request.
The middle voice of ἐσθίω (φάγομαι) emphasizes personal participation in eating; the active voice emphasizes the action itself
Dining customs in Mark: reclined at table, bread broken and shared, wine passed around
sheets.drill_instruction: Substitution Drill: Start with 'δός μοι τὸν ἄρτον' and substitute: δός μοι τὸ ποτήριον, δός μοι τὸ ἅλας, δός μοι τὸ κρέας. This builds muscle memory for the accusative object constructions.

examples.english: for every one shall be salted with fire

principles: Neuter nouns: ἔλαιον, ὕδωρ, γάλα, κρέας, ᾠόν, ποτήριον, πῦρ
Masculine nouns: ἄρτος, σῖτος, κόκκος, οἶνος, ἰχθύς, πίναξ, κλίβανος, ξέστης
Feminine nouns: τράπεζα, ζύμη, ὑδρία, σπυρίς, συκῆ, σταφυλή
sheets.drill_instruction: Substitution Drill: Teacher names a food or vessel item, students respond with accusative constructions. Example: Teacher says 'ἄρτος', students say 'δός μοι τὸν ἄρτον', 'φέρε τὸν ἄρτον', 'ἐσθίε τὸν ἄρτον', etc.

examples.english: I am drowsy from the fire
they will rest from their toils
I am going into the bedroom

principles: Neuter nouns: ἱμάτιον, τὸ ταμεῖον, ἀνάγαιον
Masculine: χιτών, κραβάττος, κοιτών
Feminine: κλίνη, χλαῖνα, σινδών, ζώνη, στρωμνή
Imperative forms: ἔγειρε! ἀνάστηθι! γρηγόρει! κοιμηθῶμεν
sheets.drill_instruction: Substitution Drill: Teacher gives imperative commands for sleep/waking actions. Example: Teacher says 'κοιμᾶσθε' (you sleep), students respond 'κοιμηθῶμεν ἤδη' (let us sleep now), 'ἀνάστηθι' (rise), etc. Builds imperative fluency for rest routines.

examples.english: the upper storey of the city

principles: Feminine: νύξ, σελήνη, λυχνία, θύρα, αὐλή, οἰκία
Neuter: σκότος, ταμεῖον, ἀνάγαιον, ὑπερῷον, δῶμα, ἐνύπνιον, ὄναρ
Masculine: ἀλέκτωρ, λύχνος, ὄρθρος, οἶκος, ὕπνος
Genitive of time: νυκτός (by night), πρωΐ (in early morning)
sheets.drill_instruction: Substitution Drill: Teacher provides time expressions, students respond with nocturnal activities. Example: Teacher says 'μεσονύκτιον', students say 'μεσονύκτιον καθεύδουσιν', 'μεσονύκτιον ἀναπαύονται', etc. Builds vocabulary for understanding Mark's night scenes and dream narratives.

examples.greek: ἀγάπη ἀγάπη, ἱερὸς ναός, βασιλεία μεγάλη
examples.english: great love, holy temple, great kingdom (adjectives modifying nouns)

principles: The sentence (περίοδος) is built from nouns (ὄνομα) and verbs (ῥῆμα)
Adjectives (ἐπίθετον) modify nouns and agree in gender, number, and case
Every clause needs a verb; nouns and adjectives support the verb
sheets.drill_instruction: Identification Drill: Read sentences from Mark and identify the core parts: τὸ ὄνομα (noun), τὸ ῥῆμα (verb), τὸ ἐπίθετον (adjective). Example: 'ὁ θεὸς ἀγαπᾷ τὸν κόσμον' — ὄνομα (θεός), ῥῆμα (ἀγαπᾷ), ὄνομα (κόσμος).

examples.greek: ὁ λόγος, ἡ ἀλήθεια, τὸ φῶς
examples.english: the word, the truth, the light (articles marking nouns)

examples.greek: ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ, εἰς τὴν οἰκίαν, ἀπὸ Ναζαρέτ
examples.english: in the temple, into the house, from Nazareth (prepositions + case)

principles: Pronouns (ἀντωνυμία) replace nouns and agree in person, number, gender
The article (ἄρθρον) marks definiteness and agrees with nouns
Prepositions (πρόθεσις) govern specific cases to show relationships
Adverbs (ἐπίρρημα) modify verbs and are indeclinable
sheets.drill_instruction: Substitution Drill: Replace nouns with pronouns; add articles to bare nouns; add prepositions before nouns to change meaning. Example: 'θεός ἀγαπᾷ κόσμος' → 'ὁ θεὸς ἀγαπᾷ τὸν κόσμον' (adding articles and case agreement).

examples.english: and, but, that, when (conjunctions linking clauses)
to say, to see, to become (verbal nouns)

principles: Conjunctions (σύνδεσμος) link equal clauses or introduce dependent clauses
Participles (μετοχή) combine verbal and adjectival functions
Infinitives (ἀπαρέμφατον) function as verbal nouns
Interjections (ἐπιφώνημα) express emotion and are indeclinable
sheets.drill_instruction: Recognition Drill: Identify participles vs. infinitives in Mark's sentences; recognize conjunctions that signal purpose, result, reason, and time. Recognize that participles modify nouns while infinitives serve as objects.

examples.english: the word of God (genitive showing possession)
I give to him (dative indirect object)

principles: Cases show the relationship of nouns to verbs and other words
Nominative = subject; Accusative = direct object; Genitive/Dative show other relationships
Each case has its own article form in all genders and numbers
sheets.drill_instruction: Case Identification Drill: Read Mark sentences and identify the case of each noun. Example: 'τὸν θεὸν ἀγαπῶ' — θεόν is accusative (object). 'ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ' — θεοῦ is genitive (possession).

paradigms.title: Noun Case Paradigm: θεός (God) - Masculine
paradigms.example: NOM: ὁ θεός (the God - subject) | GEN: τοῦ θεοῦ (of God - possession) | DAT: τῷ θεῷ (to God - indirect obj.) | ACC: τὸν θεόν (God - direct obj.) | VOC: ὦ θεέ (O God! - address)

paradigms.title: Noun Case Paradigm: ψυχή (soul) - Feminine
paradigms.example: NOM: ἡ ψυχή (the soul - subject) | GEN: τῆς ψυχῆς (of soul) | DAT: τῇ ψυχῇ (to soul) | ACC: τὴν ψυχήν (soul - object) | VOC: ὦ ψυχή (O soul!)

paradigms.title: Noun Case Paradigm: ἔργον (work) - Neuter
paradigms.example: NOM: τὸ ἔργον (the work - subject) | GEN: τοῦ ἔργου (of work) | DAT: τῷ ἔργῳ (to work) | ACC: τὸ ἔργον (work - object) | VOC: (neuter no vocative)

paradigms.title: Plural Case Paradigm: θεοί (gods)
paradigms.example: NOM: οἱ θεοί (the gods) | GEN: τῶν θεῶν (of gods) | DAT: τοῖς θεοῖς (to gods) | ACC: τοὺς θεούς (gods - object)

examples.greek: ὁ ἀνθρωπος, ὁ θεός, ὁ κύριος
ἡ γυνή, ἡ αλήθεια, ἡ ψυχή
τὸ τέκνον, τὸ φῶς, τὸ ὕδωρ

principles: Gender is grammatical (not always semantic) — learn gender with each noun
Adjectives, articles, and pronouns must agree with nouns in gender and number
Plural forms are used for 2 or more; dual (ὁ δυϊκός) is rare in Koine Greek
sheets.drill_instruction: Agreement Drill: Give a noun; student responds with agreeing article, adjective, and pronoun. Example: Teacher says 'ψυχή' → Student says 'ἡ ἁγία ψυχή, αὕτη' (feminine singular article, adjective, pronoun).

paradigms.title: Article Paradigm (Singular)
paradigms.example: MASCULINE: ὁ (the) | FEMININE: ἡ (the) | NEUTER: τό (the)

paradigms.title: Article Paradigm (Plural)
paradigms.example: MASCULINE: οἱ (the) | FEMININE: αἱ (the) | NEUTER: τά (the)

paradigms.title: Adjective Agreement: ἀγάπη (love)
paradigms.example: SINGULAR: ἡ μεγάλη ἀγάπη (the great love - fem. sg.) | PLURAL: αἱ μεγάλαι ἀγάπαι (the great loves - fem. pl.)

paradigms.title: Adjective Agreement: θεός (God)
paradigms.example: SINGULAR: ὁ μέγας θεός (the great God - masc. sg.) | PLURAL: οἱ μεγάλοι θεοί (the great gods - masc. pl.)

paradigms.title: Adjective Agreement: ἔργον (work)
paradigms.example: SINGULAR: τὸ μέγα ἔργον (the great work - neut. sg.) | PLURAL: τὰ μέγα ἔργα (the great works - neut. pl.)

principles: Greek tense emphasizes aspect (how action occurs) more than time (when)
Aorist = undefined aspect (punctiliar); Present = ongoing; Perfect = completed with result
All tenses can express past, present, or future depending on context
sheets.drill_instruction: Aspect Recognition Drill: Read Mark sentences and identify whether the tense is punctiliar (aorist), ongoing (present), or resultative (perfect). Note how aspect changes meaning.

paradigms.title: Present Indicative Paradigm (λύω - I loose/release)
paradigms.example: λύω (I loose), λύεις (you loose), λύει (he/she/it looses), λύομεν (we loose), λύετε (you all loose), λύουσι(ν) (they loose)

paradigms.title: Aorist Indicative Paradigm (ἔλυσα - I loosed)
paradigms.example: ἔλυσα (I loosed), ἔλυσας (you loosed), ἔλυσε(ν) (he loosed), ἐλύσαμεν (we loosed), ἐλύσατε (you loosed), ἔλυσαν (they loosed)

paradigms.title: Perfect Indicative Paradigm (λέλυκα - I have loosed)
paradigms.example: λέλυκα (I have loosed), λέλυκας (you have loosed), λέλυκε(ν) (he has loosed), λελύκαμεν (we have loosed), λελύκατε (you have loosed), λελύκασι(ν) (they have loosed)

examples.english: God loves the world (subject does the action)

terms.english: The middle voice (subject acts for itself)
The passive voice (subject is acted upon)

examples.greek: ὁ κόσμος ἀγαπᾶται ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ
examples.english: the world is loved by God (subject receives the action)

principles: Active = subject does the action; Passive = subject receives the action; Middle = subject acts on/for itself
Middle voice is more common in Greek than in English and needs to be recognized carefully
Passive voice often appears without an expressed agent (agent understood)
sheets.drill_instruction: Voice Conversion Drill: Convert active sentences to passive and vice versa. Example: 'Ἰησοῦς ἐδίδασκεν' (active) → 'ἐδίδασκεν ὑπὸ Ἰησοῦ' (passive equivalent).

paradigms.title: Active Voice (λύω - I loose)
paradigms.example: λύω (I loose), λύεις (you loose), λύει (he looses), λύομεν (we loose), λύετε (you loose), λύουσι(ν) (they loose)

paradigms.title: Middle Voice (λύομαι - I loose for myself)
paradigms.example: λύομαι (I loose for myself), λύῃ (you loose for yourself), λύεται (he looses for himself), λυόμεθα (we loose for ourselves), λύεσθε (you loose for yourselves), λύονται (they loose for themselves)

paradigms.title: Passive Voice (λύομαι - I am loosed)
paradigms.example: λύομαι (I am loosed), λύῃ (you are loosed), λύεται (he is loosed), λυόμεθα (we are loosed), λύεσθε (you are loosed), λύονται (they are loosed)

paradigms.title: Aorist Passive (ἐλύθην - I was loosed)
paradigms.example: ἐλύθην (I was loosed), ἐλύθης (you were loosed), ἐλύθη (he was loosed), ἐλύθημεν (we were loosed), ἐλύθητε (you were loosed), ἐλύθησαν (they were loosed)

examples.greek: ἵνα ζήσῃ (in order that he may live)

principles: Indicative states reality (past, present, future possible)
Subjunctive appears in dependent clauses and expresses contingency/potential
Imperative commands direct action (sing., plur., sometimes prohibitive)
Optative (rare in Koine) expresses wishes or remote conditions
sheets.drill_instruction: Mood Recognition Drill: Read Mark sentences and identify the mood. Note which moods appear with which particles (ἵνα with subjunctive, μή with prohibitions, etc.).

paradigms.title: Imperative Paradigm (loose! sg./pl.)
paradigms.example: λῦε (you loose!), λύετε (you all loose!) | μὴ λῦε (don't you loose!), μὴ λύετε (don't you all loose!)

paradigms.title: Subjunctive Paradigm (that I might loose)
paradigms.example: λύω (that I might loose), λύῃς (that you might loose), λύῃ (that he might loose), λύωμεν (that we might loose), λύητε (that you might loose), λύωσι(ν) (that they might loose)

paradigms.title: Optative Paradigm (if only I would loose - rare)
paradigms.example: λύοιμι (if only I would loose), λύοις (if only you would loose), λύοι (if only he would loose)

principles: Person is marked on verbs through endings (first: -ω/-μι; second: -ς/ε; third: -ει/-ουσι(ν))
Pronouns (ἐγώ, σύ, αὐτός) often repeat the person marked on the verb for emphasis
Person combines with number (singular/plural) and tense/mood to create complete verbal forms
sheets.drill_instruction: Verb Parsing Drill: Given a Greek verb, identify its person and number. Example: 'λέγουσιν' = 3rd person plural. 'λέγω' = 1st person singular.

sheets.english_title: How to Build Fluency · Six Drills
sheets.introduction: Fluency comes from producing the language, not from recognising it. Every drill below can be done alone in front of a wall sheet, or in pairs in three minutes. Little and often beats one long push.

terms.greek: Take one true statement and surround it with questions before moving on.
terms.english: The information is not the point — the repetition is.

examples.greek: τοῦτο βιβλίον ἐστίν. τί ἐστιν τοῦτο; — βιβλίον. βιβλίον ἐστὶν ἢ ποτήριον; — βιβλίον. ποῦ ἐστιν τὸ βιβλίον; — ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης. τίνος ἐστὶν τὸ βιβλίον; — ἐμόν ἐστιν.
examples.english: This is a book. What is this? — A book. Is it a book or a cup? — A book. Where is the book? — On the table. Whose is the book? — It is mine.

terms.greek: Keep the frame, change one slot. You feel the endings shift in your mouth instead of on paper.

examples.greek: ὁ Ἰησοῦς λαλεῖ. → οἱ μαθηταὶ λαλοῦσιν. → οἱ μαθηταὶ ἀκούουσιν. → ἀκούουσιν. → ἤκουον. → ἤκουσαν. → ἀκούσουσιν.
examples.english: Jesus speaks. → The disciples speak. → The disciples listen. → They listen. → They were listening. → They heard. → They will hear.

terms.greek: Describe what is around you and what people are doing, in the simplest Koine you have. Small, constant, out loud.

examples.greek: ὁ ἀδελφὸς γράφει. ἡ ἀδελφὴ ἐσθίει. ὁ λύχνος ἐπὶ τῆς τραπέζης ἐστίν. νῦν ἐσθίω· εἶτα καθευδήσω.
examples.english: The brother is writing. The sister is eating. The lamp is on the table. Now I am eating; then I will sleep.

terms.greek: One person commands, the others obey in silence. No translation, no explanation — comprehension shows up in the body before it reaches the tongue.
terms.english: Total Physical Response: action proves understanding.

examples.greek: ἔγειρε· ἐλθὲ πρὸς τὴν θύραν· ἄνοιξον αὐτήν· κάθισον. λάβε τὸ ποτήριον καὶ δὸς αὐτὸ τῷ ἀδελφῷ.
examples.english: Get up; come to the door; open it; sit down. Take the cup and give it to your brother.

terms.greek: Read a paragraph of Mark, close the book, and answer three questions aloud. Two or three sentences is plenty. This single habit exercises every tier of fluency at once.

examples.greek: τίς; τί γίνεται; διὰ τί; πρῶτον … εἶτα … καὶ εὐθύς … τέλος …
examples.english: Who is in the scene? What happens? Why? First … then … and immediately … finally …

terms.greek: Never translate the parsing question. Ask in Greek, answer in Greek, in a fixed order.

examples.greek: τί μέρος λόγου ἐστίν; — ῥῆμα. ἐν ποίῳ χρόνῳ; — ἀόριστος. ποία διάθεσις; — παθητική. ποῖον πρόσωπον; — τρίτον, ἑνικόν.
examples.english: What part of speech? — A verb. In what tense? — Aorist. What voice? — Passive. What person? — Third, singular.

sheets.rhythm: A rhythm for the fortnight: five minutes of greetings and classroom phrases · parse the day's verses aloud using nothing but Greek grammar terms · retell one paragraph of Mark and say what you think of it. Then say εὖ καθεύδοις to somebody and go to bed.
